title: Chest Pain & Possible Acute Coronary Syndrome (LVN Scope)
subtitle: 62 y/o male with sudden chest pressure radiating to the jaw and arm — the LVN must recognize possible cardiac ischemia, respond immediately within scope, and escalate to the RN/provider
nursesNote: 1330 - 62 y/o male, med-surg unit, history of hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and type 2 diabetes. Shortly after walking back from the bathroom he developed sudden chest pressure that radiates to his left arm and jaw. He is diaphoretic (cold, sweaty), short of breath, nauseated, and pale, and says 'something is really wrong.' He rates the pressure as severe. He initially thought it was 'just indigestion' after lunch. The LVN practices under the direction of the RN/provider; ordered protocols and PRN cardiac medications are on the chart.

patient.name: R. Halloran
patient.admitDate: Med-Surg; history of HTN, hyperlipidemia, type 2 diabetes

steps.title: Recognize Cues
steps.inst: Select the THREE (3) findings that MOST suggest possible acute coronary syndrome (a heart attack).

opts.text: Sudden chest pressure radiating to the left arm and jaw
opts.rat: Chest pressure with radiation to the arm and jaw is a classic sign of cardiac ischemia.

opts.text: Diaphoresis (cold sweat) with shortness of breath and nausea
opts.rat: Diaphoresis, dyspnea, and nausea commonly accompany a myocardial infarction.

opts.text: Anxiety with a feeling that 'something is really wrong' and pallor
opts.rat: A sense of impending doom with pallor is a recognized accompaniment of acute cardiac events.

opts.text: Blood glucose is mildly elevated
opts.rat: An elevated glucose reflects his diabetes (a risk factor/background) but is not the acute sign of ischemia here.

opts.text: Bowel sounds are present in all quadrants
opts.rat: Normal bowel sounds are unrelated to the cardiac concern.

opts.text: The client ate lunch about an hour ago
opts.rat: Recent eating may tempt staff to call it indigestion, but it is not a sign of ACS — and cardiac pain must not be dismissed as indigestion.

opts.text: Skin over the heels is intact
opts.rat: Intact skin is a reassuring, unrelated finding.

steps.title: Analyze Cues
steps.inst: Select the THREE (3) statements that correctly reflect the reasoning and the LVN's role.

opts.text: Chest pressure with radiation to the arm/jaw, diaphoresis, dyspnea, and nausea are classic signs of possible acute coronary syndrome and require immediate action — this is a potential emergency, not indigestion
opts.rat: These findings demand prompt recognition and response; dismissing them as indigestion is dangerous.

opts.text: The LVN stops the client's activity, keeps him at rest, stays with him, obtains vital signs, applies oxygen per order/protocol if indicated, and notifies the RN/provider immediately — recognizing and escalating without diagnosing or interpreting the ECG
opts.rat: The LVN provides immediate within-scope support and escalates; diagnosis and ECG interpretation are RN/provider functions.

opts.text: Older adults, women, and clients with diabetes may have atypical presentations (fatigue, indigestion-like discomfort, shortness of breath), so symptoms should not be dismissed
opts.rat: Atypical presentations are common in these groups; a low threshold for recognition is essential.

opts.text: Chest pain that occurs after eating is always simple indigestion and can be observed
opts.rat: Cardiac pain can mimic indigestion; it must not be assumed benign.

opts.text: The LVN should have the client walk to see whether the pain resolves
opts.rat: Activity increases cardiac oxygen demand and is dangerous during possible ischemia; the client rests.

opts.text: The LVN should independently diagnose a myocardial infarction and decide on treatment
opts.rat: Diagnosis and treatment decisions are outside the LVN's scope; the LVN recognizes and escalates.

steps.title: Prioritize
steps.inst: Drag these findings from MOST concerning (1) to LEAST (5).

opts.text: Crushing chest pressure radiating to the jaw and left arm with diaphoresis
opts.rat: Classic ischemic chest pain with diaphoresis is the most concerning — possible evolving myocardial infarction.

opts.text: Shortness of breath with oxygen saturation dropping to 94%
opts.rat: Dyspnea with falling saturation signals cardiopulmonary compromise and is highly concerning.

opts.text: Nausea and pallor
opts.rat: Associated autonomic symptoms support a serious cardiac event, though less directly than the pain and hypoxia.

opts.text: Blood pressure elevated to 158/92 with the pain
opts.rat: Elevated blood pressure often accompanies acute pain; it is monitored but less immediately dangerous than the findings above.

opts.text: General anxiety about being in the hospital
opts.rat: Least concerning as a physical cue, though anxiety can accompany a cardiac event.

steps.title: Generate Solutions
steps.inst: Select the THREE (3) actions that are appropriate and within the LVN's scope.

opts.text: Keep the client at rest in a position of comfort, obtain vital signs, and apply oxygen per order/protocol if indicated, staying with him
opts.rat: Rest reduces cardiac demand; vitals and oxygen (per order) support the client while help is summoned.

opts.text: Notify the RN/provider immediately and prepare for an ordered 12-lead ECG and ordered medications (aspirin, sublingual nitroglycerin per order)
opts.rat: Immediate escalation and preparing ordered diagnostics/medications are correct.

opts.text: Administer ordered sublingual nitroglycerin per order — checking blood pressure first (holding and reporting if below the ordered parameter) and reassessing pain and blood pressure after
opts.rat: Nitroglycerin is given per order with a blood-pressure check because it can cause hypotension; reassessment follows each dose.

opts.text: Encourage the client to walk to determine whether the pain is cardiac
opts.rat: Activity increases cardiac oxygen demand and is dangerous during possible ischemia.

opts.text: Dismiss the symptoms as indigestion and offer an antacid without notifying anyone
opts.rat: Assuming indigestion and failing to escalate can be fatal in a heart attack.

opts.text: Independently interpret the ECG and decide the client is not having a heart attack
opts.rat: Interpreting the ECG and ruling out an MI is outside the LVN's scope.

steps.title: Take Action
steps.inst: Drag the actions from FIRST (1) to LAST (5).

opts.text: Stop the client's activity, keep him at rest in a position of comfort, and stay with him (summon help using the call light)
opts.rat: FIRST — reduce cardiac demand and do not leave the client; summon help without leaving.

opts.text: Obtain vital signs and apply oxygen per order/protocol if indicated
opts.rat: SECOND — quick data and supportive oxygen while preparing to escalate.

opts.text: Notify the RN/provider immediately using SBAR
opts.rat: THIRD — escalate at once so the provider can direct emergency care.

opts.text: Administer ordered medications (aspirin, sublingual nitroglycerin) per order — checking blood pressure before nitroglycerin — and prepare for the ordered 12-lead ECG
opts.rat: FOURTH — carry out ordered emergency medications and diagnostics within scope.

opts.text: Document the event, findings, interventions, and communication, and continue close monitoring
opts.rat: LAST — document and keep monitoring the client's response.

opts.text: After rest, oxygen per order, and ordered nitroglycerin, the chest pain decreased and vital signs stabilized
opts.rat: Relief of pain with stabilized vitals suggests the interventions are helping.

opts.text: The RN/provider was notified, a 12-lead ECG was obtained, and ordered treatment was started; the LVN carried out orders within scope
opts.rat: Prompt escalation led to appropriate diagnostics and treatment implemented correctly.

opts.text: The client's chest pain worsened and spread, with increasing shortness of breath and diaphoresis despite nitroglycerin
opts.rat: Escalating symptoms despite treatment signal a worsening cardiac event — escalate immediately and prepare for emergency care.

opts.text: Staff told the client to walk off the pain, and his condition deteriorated
opts.rat: Activity during ischemia was the wrong action and worsened the client — must be corrected.

opts.text: After ordered nitroglycerin the client reports a mild headache, but the chest pain is relieved and blood pressure remains adequate
opts.rat: Headache is an expected nitroglycerin side effect; relieved chest pain with adequate blood pressure is a good response.

opts.text: The client now rests comfortably, pain-free, on the cardiac monitor with stable vital signs
opts.rat: Pain-free rest with stable monitored vitals reflects a positive outcome.

opts.text: The client remains anxious about the events but is pain-free with stable vital signs
opts.rat: Residual anxiety without physical deterioration is neither clear improvement nor worsening — provide support.

opts.text: The client's blood glucose remains mildly elevated and is being managed per orders
opts.rat: The glucose is unchanged and already being managed — not the acute cardiac concern.

reference: Aligned to the NCSBN NCLEX-PN Test Plan client-need category: Physiological Adaptation (cardiac alterations / acute coronary syndrome) using the NCSBN Clinical Judgment Measurement Model, and targeting a top LVN blueprint gap (Physiological Adaptation is 7-13% of the NCLEX-PN exam and is currently thin in the app). Concepts reflect standard nursing practice at LVN scope: recognizing typical ischemic chest pain (pressure radiating to arm/jaw, diaphoresis, dyspnea, nausea, pallor, sense of doom) and atypical presentations in older adults, women, and clients with diabetes; the immediate response (stop activity and rest, stay with the client, obtain vital signs, apply oxygen per order/protocol, notify the RN/provider immediately, prepare for an ordered 12-lead ECG, and administer ordered aspirin and sublingual nitroglycerin per order with a blood-pressure check because nitroglycerin can cause hypotension and headache); and the scope boundary that the LVN recognizes and escalates but does not diagnose a myocardial infarction or interpret the ECG. Specific nitroglycerin dosing/frequency and blood-pressure hold parameters follow the provider's order and facility protocol and are not asserted here. Apply within current BVNPT regulations and facility policy, which can change. Lab and vital-sign values use standard reference ranges and are illustrative for the scenario; exact clinical figures are marked for faculty confirmation.
